title: Ireland at the Top of the World: How a Small Nation Became Rugby's Dominant Force
summary: Ireland's rise to the top of World Rugby rankings is one of sport's most remarkable stories. With back-to-back Grand Slams, record winning streaks and a historic series win over New Zealand, Andy Farrell's side have redefined what's possible for a nation of 5 million people.
content:
Ireland is a small country. Its population is just over five million people. Its rugby infrastructure, while passionate and well-organised, cannot compare in depth to England, France, or the southern hemisphere giants. And yet, in the mid-2020s, Ireland sits at the top of the World Rugby rankings and plays some of the most compelling team rugby on the planet.

How did this happen? And can it last?

The Foundation: Province as Nation

Irish rugby's strength comes from its provinces. Leinster, Munster, Ulster, and Connacht compete in the European Champions Cup and the United Rugby Championship against the best clubs in the world. The standard is high. The experience is real. And crucially, the players who make up the Irish national team spend most of their careers competing against — and beating — world-class opposition at club level.

Leinster, in particular, have been the spine of this Irish team. The players who learned to play under Joe Schmidt at Leinster — to execute detailed game plans under pressure, to understand the game's patterns deeply enough to adapt in real time — brought that education to the national team. And when Schmidt became Ireland head coach, he was coaching players who already understood what he was asking of them.

The Schmidt Blueprint

Joe Schmidt's Ireland redefined how the national team played. The game plan was precise, detail-oriented, and executed with a consistency that left opponents unable to find weaknesses. Ireland under Schmidt won three Six Nations titles, beat the All Blacks for the first time in Irish history, and consistently performed above expectations on the world stage.

But the ultimate prize — a World Cup — escaped them. Quarter-final exits in 2015 and 2019 left a painful question hanging over Schmidt's otherwise extraordinary legacy: could this Ireland team perform when it mattered most?

What you build over time — the trust, the understanding, the belief that everyone in the team will do their job even when it's hard — that is what allows you to win the big matches. It doesn't happen by accident. It is the product of years of work. — Andy Farrell

Farrell's Evolution

Andy Farrell, Schmidt's successor, inherited a good team and made it great. The tactical framework remained — Ireland still play a structured, disciplined game — but Farrell added an intensity and a physical edge that Schmidt's side had occasionally lacked. And he built a squad depth that Ireland had never previously had, allowing the team to maintain their level across a full season and a full year of Test rugby.

The results have been extraordinary. Back-to-back Six Nations Grand Slams. A historic series win over the All Blacks in New Zealand. A World Rugby number one ranking that has been defended consistently. And perhaps most importantly, a belief in the squad and the country that this Irish team is not just having a good run — it is genuinely one of the best teams in the world.

The Players Who Made It Possible

Jonathan Sexton's leadership and game management defined an era. Tadhg Furlong is widely considered the best tighthead prop in world rugby. Peter O'Mahony's experience and physicality provide an edge that younger teams cannot manufacture. And behind them, a generation of players — Hugo Keenan, James Lowe, Mack Hansen — who have added pace, power, and creativity to what was already a formidable foundation.

The World Cup Question

The one trophy that has eluded Ireland remains the Rugby World Cup. The 2023 edition in France saw Ireland go into the tournament as the world's number one team and favourites in many assessments — and exit in the quarter-finals to South Africa, the eventual champions, in a match where the margins were desperately fine.

That defeat hurt. But it did not break anything. Ireland continue to play at the top of the world game, to develop players who can compete with anyone, and to build on the foundations that have made them one of sport's most compelling success stories.

For a nation of five million people, that is something remarkable. And it is nowhere near finished.
